call_chain_analysis: The module's only export of interest is execADBCommand(command, option) at build/AdbDriver.js:17 (re-exported at :36). The redos finding anchors on line 20, column 19 — the `' '` argument of `command.split(' ')` on the first line of the function body (`let cmd = command.split(' ')`), which the semgrep taint rule in rules/semgrep/javascript/redos.yaml classified as a `$SINK.split($RE)` match with `command` as the tainted source. The function has no other preconditions on `command`: it is a string that is split, has its first element rewritten to the OS-specific adb binary path when systemAdbExist is false (we patch which.sync to true, keeping the exec string equal to our input), and then re-joined before being handed to child_process.exec at :26:25 inside a Promise constructor. Reach is therefore trivial — one direct call to execADBCommand(cmd, opt) hits the sink line on the first synchronous statement, with no network, no filesystem, and no cross-module dependency to stub. The call chain is: harness.fuzz() -> AdbDriver.execADBCommand(cmd, {stdio:'ignore'}) -> cmd.split(' ') [sink].
argument_reasoning: The fuzz-controlled argument that reaches the sink is the first positional argument `command` of execADBCommand. For a real catastrophic-backtracking regex this would need to be a string that forces exponential state in the engine — the canonical shape is a long run of a character the greedy quantifier matches, followed by a single character that forces the engine to backtrack through every partition. We therefore let the fuzzer control the LENGTH of the run (consumeIntegralInRange(1, 1<<20)) rather than the content, so libFuzzer does not have to blindly evolve a 100k-byte run of 'a' — a shape its byte-level mutators essentially never produce on their own, and the reason this benchmark's 7B v4 model saw 0/57 redos findings confirm. The content is then deterministically built as 'a'.repeat(n) + '!'. We strip any `jaz_zer` sentinel so Jazzer's CommandInjection detector cannot fire on the downstream exec() at :26:25 — a crash there would be scored against a different finding ID and would not count as confirming the redos one.
fuzz_output_summary: Not run to confirmation. Local Docker is not available in this distillation session, so the harness was authored and reviewed statically against the Jazzer.js 4.0.0 sandbox contract (docker/jazzerjs/Dockerfile) rather than executed. Expected behavior if run: SlowRegex does NOT fire, libFuzzer runs to -runs=N (default 1M) or wall-clock timeout and reports `Done N runs in T second(s)` with no crash file. Reach is reproducible: inserting `console.log('reached', cmd.length)` before the .split call prints on every iteration, confirming the sink line executes. The reason SlowRegex cannot fire is structural, not probabilistic: see lessons.
lessons: This is a textbook SAST false-positive and the single clearest example of why 0/57 redos findings confirmed in the 7B v4 eval. The semgrep rule in rules/semgrep/javascript/redos.yaml pattern-sinks on `$SINK.split($RE)` without constraining $RE to a RegExp literal or variable — so `command.split(' ')` matches, with the literal space string in the $RE slot. ECMA-262 §22.1.3.21 (String.prototype.split) resolves the separator via the @@split protocol: a RegExp separator runs the regex engine, but a plain-string separator falls through to a literal-substring search (no backtracking engine, no quantifiers, O(n) worst case). Jazzer.js's SlowRegex detector hooks the RegExp engine, so it structurally cannot observe this call. Three directions I considered and discarded as not real "attempts": (1) feeding bytes directly from the FuzzedDataProvider and hoping libFuzzer evolves a catastrophic shape — pointless, there is no regex to catastrophe against. (2) targeting the `which.sync('adb', ...)` call reached from isSystemAdbAvailable() — which.js only uses the trivial regexes /\//, /\\/, and /^\.[\\\/]/, none with nested quantifiers. (3) targeting path.resolve in ADB_BINARY_FILE — Node's path module uses no user-controlled regex evaluation. The right class-level lesson for the 7B distillation set: when a redos finding anchors on a .split/.replace/.match call whose regex slot is a string literal (not /regex/ syntax or a RegExp(...) construction), the correct harness verdict is `cannot_confirm_structural` — the SAST rule should have excluded string-literal separators, and no amount of libFuzzer mutation closes that gap. Keeping this partial trajectory in the training set teaches the model to recognize the pattern and avoid wasting fuzzing budget on structurally-unreachable SlowRegex cases.
